subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday. Arnab lay awake imagining rain, cold, hunger, darkness. In the morning he crammed two jackets, three snacks and his father's big torch into his bag.
Monday. At the school gate the bag dragged him sideways. Leela Ma'am hoisted it and raised an eyebrow. "What is in here, Arnab?" She had him leave half of it in the staff room. He watched a jacket and the torch vanish into a cupboard, feeling silly.
Tuesday. In class Leela Ma'am asked how the trip went. "My shoulders hurt at the start," Arnab said. "I never needed the torch."

qa.q: What did Arnab put in his bag on Sunday?
qa.a: He put in two jackets, three snacks and his father's big torch.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling as the jacket and torch vanished into the cupboard?
qa.a: He felt silly, and probably a little embarrassed, since his worry had loaded him with things that were taken away.

qa.q: What could Arnab try next time instead of packing for everything, and why?
qa.a: He could list the likely needs and ask the teacher what is really needed, so his worry gets a limit and his bag stays light.

qa.q: How does Leela Ma'am see Arnab's packing?
qa.a: She sees a worried child carrying more than he can manage, so she lightens the load kindly and asks about the day afterwards.

grounding: A boy packs for every possible problem, ends up with a heavy bag and has to leave half of it at school.

subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage: Yash, you want to take three bags on a one-day trip? Let your Yusuf Nana tell you a story. When I was a boy, our school went to the zoo, and I was so worried about everything that might go wrong. What if I got hungry? Three snacks. What if it got cold? Two jackets. What if it got dark? The big torch from the store room. My bag was so heavy I walked sideways. At the school gate, my teacher lifted it and her eyebrows went up. "Yusuf, are you moving house?" She made me leave half of it in the classroom. I was angry that day. But without all that weight, I climbed up to the bird house with everyone else.

qa.q: What did young Yusuf take in case it got dark?
qa.a: The big torch from the store room.

qa.q: How did young Yusuf feel when the teacher made him leave half?
qa.a: Young Yusuf felt angry, though later glad to climb with everyone else.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the day better, and what could Yusuf have done instead?
qa.a: Leaving half at school was the turning point; Yusuf could have asked what was really needed and packed only that.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen the heavy bag?
qa.a: The teacher was surprised and a little amused, but also worried he wouldn't manage it all day.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy worried about what might go wrong, packing too much and having to leave half at school.

subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage: Hrithik had packed for the school trip to the hill fort as if he were leaving for a month: three snack boxes, two jackets, a big torch, a first-aid tin, a book, and a board game. It was already hot and the bus was late. When his teacher, Salma ma'am, lifted his bag onto the bus steps, she nearly dropped it. "Hrithik, what if you can't carry this up the hill?" He had worried about everything except that. She asked him to keep one snack, one jacket and water, and leave the rest in the staffroom. He felt his face go red. But at the top of the hill, sweaty and puffing, he was glad his bag was light, and nobody asked about his torch.

qa.q: How many snack boxes did Hrithik pack?
How did Hrithik feel when Salma ma'am asked him to leave things behind?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face going red, since he had worried about everything except the weight.

qa.q: What else could Hrithik try next time he feels worried about what might go wrong?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher or a parent which worries are real, and pack one item for each instead of several.

qa.q: How does the heavy bag look to Salma ma'am?
qa.a: Salma ma'am sees a worried boy about to struggle up a hill, so she kindly helps him cut down.

grounding: It shows a boy so worried about what might go wrong that he packs far too much, and the teacher asks him to leave half at school.
